title: Human Rights and Multicultural Rights

cards.h: Rights for humans, rights for groups
cards.b:
This lesson has two parts. The first is human rights: rights claimed by every person simply as a human being, set out in international law. The second is multicultural rights: special rights for cultural, religious or ethnic groups inside a state.

They seem to pull in different directions. Human rights are universal and individual. Multicultural rights are group-specific. The big debate is whether group rights can sit with individual liberty.

Both feature in Paper I (theory) and, through the Constitution, in Paper I Section B (minority rights, Articles 29-30, personal laws). In Paper II, human rights link to the UN, R2P and humanitarian intervention. Keep these links in mind.

Human rights are claimed by all people on the basis of humanity: universal, inalienable, indivisible and equal. They grew from natural rights, but after the horrors of the Second World War they became a matter of international law.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. It is not a treaty but is now widely seen as customary law.

cards.h: The International Bill of Human Rights
cards.b:
• UDHR (1948): 30 articles, covering both civil-political and economic-social rights.
  • ICCPR (International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966, in force 1976).
  • ICESCR (International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966, in force 1976).

The Cold War split the two covenants: the West stressed civil-political rights, the Soviet bloc stressed economic-social rights. India has ratified both covenants (1979).

Later treaties cover racial discrimination (1965), women (CEDAW, 1979), torture (1984), children (1989) and disability (2006). The Vienna Declaration (1993) said all rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated.

The UN Human Rights Council (2006) replaced the Commission on Human Rights, and has a Universal Periodic Review of every state.

• Universalists: rights flow from shared human dignity. If rights depend on culture, tyrants can excuse abuses by pointing to tradition.
  • Relativists: the UDHR reflects Western liberal values. Cultures differ on the individual and community. Some states, such as Singapore and Malaysia in the 1990s, pushed "Asian values": order and community before individual freedom. The 1993 Bangkok Declaration reflected this.
  • Amartya Sen, "Human Rights and Asian Values" (1997): Asia is too diverse for one set of values, and tolerance and liberty have deep roots in Asian history (Ashoka, Akbar).
  • Middle paths: Abdullahi An-Naim seeks cross-cultural dialogue. Jack Donnelly speaks of "relative universality".

Note too the Third World argument: the right to development and economic justice cannot be ignored.

• Marxist: rights ignore economic structures.
  • Feminist: the public-private divide let violence at home go unseen. Rights have been framed in male terms. The campaign "women's rights are human rights" and CEDAW respond.
  • Postcolonial: used selectively by powerful states to justify intervention. Makau Mutua speaks of a "savages-victims-saviours" pattern.
  • Enforcement gap: there is no world government. Treaties rely on state consent and weak monitoring bodies.
  • Sovereignty clash: humanitarian intervention (Kosovo 1999, Libya 2011) and the Responsibility to Protect (UN World Summit, 2005) raise old doubts.

Defenders say that the rights regime still gives victims a language and a weapon, even if imperfect.

Multiculturalism accepts that modern societies hold many cultures, and that fair treatment may require recognising differences, not ignoring them.

The liberal tradition says: treat everyone as an individual and be "difference-blind". Multiculturalists say that a neutral state is not neutral. A public holiday on Sunday, the language of schools and rules on dress all favour the majority culture.

Charles Taylor, "The Politics of Recognition" (1992): misrecognition can harm people. A fair state needs a politics of recognition, not just of equal rights. He pointed to Quebec's language laws.

Iris Marion Young, Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990): group-differentiated citizenship and special representation for oppressed groups.

Will Kymlicka, Multicultural Citizenship (1995), gives the best-known liberal defence. Culture is the context in which people make choices, so individuals have an interest in their cultural membership. He proposes three kinds of group-differentiated rights.

Self-government rights

For national minorities such as indigenous peoples or Quebec: autonomy, territory, language.

Polyethnic rights

For immigrant groups: exemption from rules (e.g., turban for Sikh police in Canada), funding for cultural practices.

Special representation rights

Reserved seats or places for disadvantaged groups.

He separates external protections (a group's shield against the majority, acceptable) from internal restrictions (a group's power over its own members, which liberals must reject).

• Brian Barry, Culture and Equality (2001): equal rules for all are fairer. Exemptions give an advantage to those with the loudest claim.
  • Susan Okin, "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?" (1999): group rights often protect practices that harm women, as the private sphere is where cultures control women.
  • Chandran Kukathas: individuals should be free to leave a group. Groups have no rights beyond individuals' freedom of association.
  • Bhikhu Parekh, Rethinking Multiculturalism (2000): defends a dialogue-based multiculturalism. No culture is perfect, and each should be open to criticism from others, within an "operative public values" framework.
  • Habermas argues that equal rights already protect cultural identity if properly interpreted.

Fears of social fragmentation led several European leaders to declare multiculturalism a failure around 2010-11.

cards.h: Human rights and minority rights in India
cards.b:
• Institutions: Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 created the NHRC (October 1993) and State commissions. It was amended in 2006 and 2019. The NHRC can recommend, but its orders are not binding.
  • Courts: Vishaka (1997) used CEDAW to fill a legal gap. The Supreme Court uses international norms where they do not conflict with domestic law.
  • Minority rights: Article 29 (protection of language and culture of any section), Article 30 (minorities' right to set up and run educational institutions), T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002), Articles 25-28 on religion.

cards.h: Tribal rights, personal laws and the Indian model
cards.b:
• Tribal rights: Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA (1996), the Forest Rights Act (2006), and Articles 371 provisions for specific States.
  • Personal laws: Shah Bano (1985), Shayara Bano (2017) and Article 44. Uttarakhand passed a Uniform Civil Code law in 2024, in force since January 2025.
  • India's model is sometimes called "constitutional multiculturalism", mixing group recognition (Articles 29-30, reservations) with a push for individual equality and reform.

"Human rights are universal in appeal but culturally contested." Discuss.
Examine Kymlicka's theory of multicultural citizenship.
Are group rights compatible with individual liberty? Illustrate with the Indian case.
Assess the role of the NHRC in protecting human rights in India.

Structure: for the first part, give the UDHR and two covenants, universalism versus relativism (with Sen), and critiques. For the second, argue from the limits of difference-blind liberalism: Taylor, Young, Kymlicka and his three rights, then Barry, Okin and Kukathas against. Use India as a worked example: Articles 29-30, Fifth and Sixth Schedules, personal laws and the UCC debate. Sum up with a balanced, dialogue-based position.

quiz.w: By the UN General Assembly; observed as Human Rights Day.

quiz.q: Which covenants form the International Bill of Human Rights along with the UDHR?
The Vienna Declaration (1993) declared that human rights are…
quiz.w: It reaffirmed the unity of all rights.
He argued Asia is diverse and has liberal traditions.
Recognition of identity is a vital human need.

quiz.q: The distinction between external protections and internal restrictions is by…
quiz.w: He accepts the first, not the second.

quiz.q: Which author asked whether multiculturalism is bad for women?
The NHRC was set up under the…
Article 30 of the Indian Constitution protects…
o: Minorities' right to establish and run educational institutions
quiz.w: Minorities based on religion or language.
